q.intro.text: A house plan uses the scale one inch to eight feet. The living room wall is twenty feet long. How long is it on the plan? Pick an answer, and say how sure you are.

e.intro.text: Four steps. Press each one. The picture moves first, then the maths on the board.

e.step0.text: Drawing first. One inch on the plan stands for eight feet. Each inch more is eight feet more, so plan to actual is times eight.

e.step1.text: Here we know the actual length and want the plan length. That's the step back. It undoes times eight with the same factor: divide by eight.

e.step2.text: Twenty divided by eight is two point five. The wall is two point five inches on the plan, straight above twenty feet.

e.step3.text: Check by going back. Two point five times eight is twenty feet. And two point five inches is two and a half inches, a half inch mark on the ruler. Draw the wall to it.

e.why.text: Quick check. Why divide by eight here, and not multiply?

e.why.ok.text: Yes. Times eight is the way from the plan to the real wall. Coming back, divide.

e.why.times.text: Times eight would give a hundred and sixty inches of paper. That's over thirteen feet for one wall. The step back divides.

e.why.add.text: A scale multiplies. It never adds. Each inch is eight feet, so two inches is sixteen feet, not nine.

t.intro.text: Your turn, same plan. The bedroom wall is two point two five inches on the plan. How long is the real wall? The first step is done for you.

t.way.text: Which step takes the plan length to the actual length?

t.way.ok.text: Yes. Plan to actual is times eight. The real wall is the long one.

t.way.div.text: Dividing goes back from feet to the plan. Here we go from the plan to the real wall.

t.way.add.text: A scale multiplies. Each inch is eight feet. Adding keeps the gap, not the scale.

t.calc.text: How long is the real wall? Two point two five times eight is what?

t.calc.ok.text: Right. Two point two five times eight is eighteen feet. Two times eight is sixteen, and zero point two five times eight is two.

t.calc.part.text: Sixteen point two five multiplies only the two. The quarter inch needs times eight too. A quarter times eight is two feet.

t.calc.div.text: That divides. Plan to actual multiplies. Each inch is eight feet.

t.calc.add.text: That adds seven. A scale multiplies: two point two five times eight.

t.calc.miss.text: Multiply both parts. Two times eight, and zero point two five times eight.

t.back.text: Check it by going back. Eighteen feet is how many inches on the plan?

t.back.ok.text: Yes. Eighteen divided by eight is two point two five inches. Back where we started, so eighteen feet is right.

t.back.times.text: A hundred and forty-four multiplies again. Going back undoes times eight. Divide.

t.back.whole.text: Eighteen divided by eight does not stop at two with a remainder. Keep going. Two divided by eight is zero point two five.

t.back.miss.text: Eighteen divided by eight is what? Keep going after the decimal point.

q.cb.right.text: At the start you picked two point five inches, and you were right. Now you can show why: the step back divides by eight.

q.cb.times.text: At the start you picked a hundred and sixty inches. That multiplies on the way back. Feet to plan inches divides by eight.

q.cb.add.text: At the start you picked thirteen inches. That adds instead of multiplying. A scale is times eight one way, and divided by eight the other.

q.cb.none.text: One scale, two directions. Times eight to the real thing, divided by eight back to the plan.

p.intro.text: Sam builds a model shed at one to forty-eight. The real shed is twelve feet long. Sam writes: twelve divided by forty-eight is zero point two five, so the model is zero point two five inches long. Is Sam right?

p.test.text: Let's test it. Build the argument, and see where it leads.

p.build.text: Now prove it. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true.

p.c1.text: Right. Straight above twelve feet, the model line is far past zero point two five. Sam's zero point two five is in feet, not inches.

p.c2.text: Right. One to forty-eight needs one unit on both sides. Twelve feet is a hundred and forty-four inches.

p.c3.text: Right. A hundred and forty-four divided by forty-eight is three. The model is three inches long. And a quarter of a foot is three inches too.

p.no.order.text: Sam may divide first. Twelve divided by forty-eight is zero point two five, and that's right, in feet. His slip is the label, not the order.

p.no.ten.text: A foot is twelve inches, not ten. A quarter of a foot is three inches.

p.no.other.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line. Which reason makes this line true?

p.done.text: That's a proof. Three claims, each with its reason, and the lines back every one. Sam's number was right. His unit was not.
